description:
Somos un equipo formado por ingenieros industriales y desarrolladores de videojuegos. Tenemos ganas de pasarlo bien y crear un proyecto que sea tanto divertido como educativo.

Equipo formado por: María Aliaga, Alejandro Andrade, Sofía Bascuas, Mario Gavín, Pedro Jato.

:D
summary: ASTRAVEL is a retro mission-control game that puts you in the chair of a space mission engineer. Choose one of four missions inspired by real NASA projects: a CubeSat that watches solar flares (MinXSS), a living yeast experiment aboard the ISS (BioNutrients), a soft landing on the Moon (Apollo 11, CLPS) and an infrared asteroid hunt past Mars (NEO Surveyor, Dawn). Build your spacecraft from 20 modules (launcher, energy, communications and payload) while you balance budget, mass, power, data downlink, mission time and a hidden risk. Then press Launch and watch the flight. Every choice has a consequence: an uncertified battery shorts out during launch, a CubeSat carrying radioactive fuel is scrubbed by range safety, and a lander without braking thrusters crashes. If you make it, a hands-on minigame waits at the destination. Each mission has several winning designs, never just one, and every failure explains why, using real engineering rules. NASAbemos? turns the trade-offs NASA engineers face every day into a game anyone can learn from in minutes.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

ASTRAVEL is a mission-design game about trade-offs. The player is an engineer in a retro, black-and-green mission control room. The game loop has four steps:

1. Mission select.

There are four missions, each based on real NASA work:

   - A "Solar Pulse": a 3U CubeSat in low Earth orbit that studies solar X-ray flares (MinXSS, CubeSat Launch Initiative).

   - B "Bio Orbit": take living yeast to the ISS, keep it incubated at 30-42 °C and bring the samples home (BioNutrients).

   - C "Project Lunaris": brake, land softly on the Moon and scan the surface (Apollo 11, CLPS).

   - D "Astro Hunt": fly past Mars to the asteroid belt and hunt asteroids in infrared (NEO Surveyor, Dawn).

   Each mission has a budget ($500k to $4M), a mass limit, a time limit and a minimum amount of science data.

2. Workshop (Taller).

The player builds the craft from four slots: Launch, Energy, Comms and Operations (payload). Each slot has five modules, so there are 625 possible craft. Six live variables show the effect of every choice: cost, mass, power balance, data produced, downlink capacity and months of work. Every module has a tooltip with a real fact, for example "The PB-NUK works like the MMRTG that powers Curiosity and Perseverance". The game shows an estimated success percentage, but it hides the risk of each module and the mission rules, just as a real design review reveals problems you did not see coming.

3. Flight (Vuelo).

A short launch animation shows what happens to the design. Red problems always end the mission. They can be numeric (the launcher cannot reach the destination, the craft is too heavy, power covers less than 40 % of demand) or rule-based (pressurised tanks near the crewed ISS, a radioisotope generator on a CubeSat ride-share, heavy armour that breaks NASA's orbital debris rules, no heat shield for returning samples). Yellow problems let the craft fly with anomalies and a higher failure chance. The flight always explains the reason in plain words.

4. Destination minigame.

A successful flight ends in a hands-on challenge based on the mission's science:

   - Ondas (A): match solar signals on an oscilloscope by tuning amplitude, frequency and phase.

   - Bio (B): keep six yeast trays alive with timing-based checks.

   - Alunizaje (C): land with side thrusters while you manage fuel, wind and the main engine. The lander is the payload module the player chose.

   - Asteroides (D): identify the target asteroid among debris, as an infrared survey would.

HOW IT WORKS (TECHNICAL)

 - Engine: Unity 6 (6000.3), C#, Universal Render Pipeline 2D, TextMeshPro.

- Data-driven design: all missions, modules and rules live in CSV files (craft_missions.csv, craft_modules.csv, craft_rules.csv). Designers and researchers change the science without touching code, and every module row cites the real hardware it represents.

- Clean architecture: the mission logic (CraftEvaluator, CraftFlightPlanner) is pure C# with no Unity dependency. It is deterministic and testable, and Unity components only display the result.

- Outcome model: failure chance = 1 % + 0.8 x (module risk above the optimal design) + 7 % per yellow issue + 4 % if the mass margin is under 35 % + 4 % if the power margin is under 35 % + 3 % if the budget reserve is under 10 %. Solar modules give half their power in the asteroid belt, because sunlight weakens with distance from the Sun.

- Automated tests: EditMode unit tests prove that every mission has an optimal design at 99 % success and other ways to win (A: 2, B: 10, C: 13, D: 9 winning designs). This guarantees there is never a single "correct answer".

- Editor tools: custom Unity menu builders assemble and wire the scenes and the module art automatically, so artists and programmers work in parallel.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- It teaches by consequence. Players learn why real missions use certified batteries, why the Moon needs braking thrusters and no parachute, why deep-space probes use nuclear power, and why the downlink must carry the science data. They learn it by failing, not from a lecture.

- It shows that engineering is about compromise. Budget, mass, power, data and time pull against each other, as they do in real missions, and players learn to look for a balanced design instead of the "best" part.

- It connects players to real NASA programmes (CubeSat Launch Initiative, BioNutrients, CLPS, NEO Surveyor, Dawn, the Deep Space Network, Radioisotope Power Systems and NASA's orbital debris rules) and invites them to read more.

- It is short and accessible: one mission takes a few minutes and needs no prior knowledge, so it fits classrooms, outreach events and science museums.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- Hidden rules: the player never sees the mission rules while building. The flight reveals them, which feels like a real launch-readiness review.

- Every mission ends at the destination with a minigame based on its science, so the reward for a good design is doing the science.

- Each slot includes a tempting "shortcut" module (an undamped prototype, a homemade battery, an armoured bus with no attitude control, an overloaded payload with no licences). Each one shows a real reason why missions fail.

- A retro CRT mission-control look with original line-art drawings for every module.

FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

- Scientific validity: module values and rules are based on real mission constraints (CubeSat ride-share rules, ISS safety, debris mitigation, lunar descent, solar power versus distance).

- Several winning designs per mission, checked by automated tests, so curious players can experiment.

- Clear feedback: every failure names its cause in plain words, so the player knows what to change and can try again.

- Ease of change: the CSV data lets non-programmers adjust the game.

- Accessibility: English interface, short sessions, simple controls.

- NASA branding rules: the game uses no NASA logos, insignia, flags or mission patches and does not imply NASA endorsement.
